449.title: Living ashtpadi 3
449.hook: the Name first, and deeds to match it
449.howItsDone: Sikh teaching pairs naam japna (remembering God) with kirat karni (honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing), so that remembrance shows up in action.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dharam, and your line: name and pure deeds. Today, living the third ashtpadi.

Let's get coffee soon, says the friend, and the coffee never happens. A company's website is full of the word integrity. A Sunday-night promise: this week will be different. Words are easy. They cost nothing until someone has to live inside them, and being let down by words that never became deeds is its own small ache. The third ashtpadi of Sukhmani is, in the end, about closing that gap.
screen: `LET'S GET COFFEE SOON.` → `INTEGRITY ON THE WEBSITE.` → `THE GAP BETWEEN WORD AND DEED.`

segments.voice: Gather the third ashtpadi. Its salok: I have searched many scriptures, and nothing equals the Name. Its long list: chanting, fasting, ritual, pilgrimage, forest, fire; none equal reflecting on the Name, because washing the body doesn't wash the mind. And its final ladder: the highest way is to chant the Name and do pure deeds. Side by side, a shape appears. The ashtpadi is suspicious of outside without inside, the ritual done while pride sits untouched. But it's just as clear that the inside has to come out. The Name first, then deeds to match. Nirmal karam, clean action, sits beside remembering at the top of the ladder. Guru Nanak puts it in one line in Sri Raag. In paraphrase: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living. Not truth as an idea you agree with; truth as a way you live. On an ordinary day, that's the Name on your lips in the morning, and the same Name visible in how you treat the cashier, the coworker, the person in the next car. Sikh teaching builds this into everyday life: naam japna, remembering the Name, sits next to kirat karni, honest work, and vand chhakna, sharing what you have. Remembering, earning, sharing: words and deeds, together.
screen: `THE SALOK, THE LIST, THE LADDER.` · `OUTSIDE WITHOUT INSIDE FAILS.` · `HIGHER STILL: TRUTHFUL LIVING.` · `REMEMBER, WORK HONESTLY, SHARE.` · then, large: `SAY IT, DO IT.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've said recently and haven't done yet, I'll call you, I'll help with that, and hold it in mind for a breath, without guilt, just looking at it. Then picture the one small step that would make the word true, and if you pray, say Waheguru once and let the word and the deed meet.
Karam, action: Sukhmani's third section in daily life, the Name first, and deeds to match it, because truthful living is higher still.
Your line: say it, do it. The call you promised can still happen. Until tomorrow.

450.title: Ashtpadi 4, salok: O virtueless one
450.hook: O ignorant and virtueless one, always remember the Lord who made you (Sukhmani 4)
450.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this salok at the start of the fourth ashtpadi; its humble address to the self is a familiar note in Gurbani, where the Gurus often speak to their own minds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karam, and your line: say it, do it. Today, the fourth ashtpadi, and a salok that doesn't flatter anyone.

A lot of self-help begins by telling you how great you are. You're enough. You've got this. There's a place for that. But there's another kind of honesty some people find more freeing: the friend who says, gently, you got this one wrong. The doctor who tells you the real number. The fourth ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens with that kind of honesty. Its first words aren't a compliment; they're an address almost no one would choose for themselves. And then, two lines later, a way home.
screen: `YOU'RE ENOUGH. YOU'VE GOT THIS.` → `THE FRIEND WHO TELLS THE TRUTH.` → `AN ADDRESS NO ONE WOULD CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok, in paraphrase: O you without virtue, O ignorant one, keep that God always in your mind. Keep in your awareness the One who made you; Nanak, only that One will stand by you to the end. The opening word, nirguniaar, means one with no virtues, nothing good of one's own to show. Iaaniaa means childish, ignorant, someone who doesn't yet understand. Hard words. But listen to who they're addressed to. Not some other, worse person. Guru Arjan speaks to the listener, and in Gurbani the Gurus speak this way to their own minds as often as to anyone. Sikhs hear it as the Guru speaking to every human being, himself included. And the salok isn't scolding for its own sake. Look at what it asks: remember. Not first become virtuous, then you may remember God. The other way round. You with nothing to show, remember the One who made you. The virtue comes from the remembering. Then the promise: nibhee naal, the One will stand by you, keep faith with you all the way. People leave; a body fails; the salok says the Maker doesn't. One more thing about the word. Gun means quality or virtue, and Gurbani uses nirgun in two directions. Of a person, it can mean without virtue, as here. Of God, it means beyond all qualities, beyond anything that can be described. Same root, two very different meanings, and this salok uses only the first.
screen: `NIRGUNIAAR: ONE WITHOUT VIRTUE.` · `THE GURU ADDRESSES EVERY MIND.` · `REMEMBER FIRST; VIRTUE FOLLOWS.` · `NIBHEE NAAL: THE ONE STANDS BY YOU.` · then, large: `REMEMBER WHO MADE YOU.`

segments.voice: Let yourself be exactly as you are today, with no achievements or good deeds to point to, just a person breathing. If you pray, bring to mind the One who made you and say Waheguru once; if not, think of all that had to happen for you to exist, and hold that in wonder, empty-handed, for a few breaths.
Nirgun, without qualities: Sukhmani's fourth section, whose salok calls out to the one without virtue, keep in mind the One who made you, who alone stands by you to the end.
Your line: remember who made you. Empty hands are enough to start. Four hundred fifty days now.

451.title: The ungrateful guest
451.hook: He gave you life, food and body, and you forget Him (Sukhmani 4)
451.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite these stanzas of the fourth ashtpadi, and Sikh practice turns their lesson into habit through shukrana, giving thanks to Waheguru, in daily prayer and the Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nirgun, and your line: remember who made you, even empty-handed. Today, the stanzas that list what was given.

A guest stays a week. The hosts give up their best room. They cook every meal, wash the towels, drive the guest to the airport at dawn. And the guest leaves without saying thank you, without even remembering the hosts' names by the time the plane lands. Sukhmani never uses the word guest in these stanzas. But the fourth ashtpadi tells a story very like it, and the guest is the human being, any one of us, fed and housed and carried, and forgetting the host.
screen: `A GUEST WHO STAYS A WEEK.` → `NO THANK-YOU, NOT EVEN A NAME.` → `THE GUEST IS ANY ONE OF US.`

segments.voice: The first stanza walks through a whole life, in paraphrase. Think of the virtues of the all-pervading One, O mortal: from what beginnings were you made? The One who formed you, shaped you and adorned you, who kept you safe in the fire of the womb. In infancy, gave you milk to drink. In the fullness of youth, food, comfort and understanding. And in old age, family and friends gather round to feed you as you sit. Then the turn: this one without virtue doesn't appreciate a single good thing done for them; only if You forgive, says Nanak, are they accepted. The next stanza lists what an ordinary day is made of. By whose grace you live at ease on the earth, laughing with children, siblings, friends and spouse. By whose grace you drink cool water, and have the gentle breeze and priceless fire. By whose grace you enjoy every pleasure. Who gave you hands and feet, ears, eyes and a tongue. And you forsake that One, and attach yourself to others. Notice what's on the list. Not miracles. Milk. Water. A breeze. Laughter with family. Hands. Things so ordinary they're noticed only when they're gone. Ingratitude, here, isn't usually cruelty. It's forgetfulness: the guest who never noticed who made the bed. And the cure is just as ordinary. Notice the giver.

segments.voice: Pick three ordinary gifts from the stanza that you have right now: water you drank today, hands that work, someone who made you laugh this week. For each one, breathe in and notice it as if for the first time, and breathe out with thanks, adding Waheguru if you pray, to the One the stanza calls the giver.
Daataa, the giver: Sukhmani's fourth ashtpadi says the One gave you the womb's shelter, milk, youth, water, breeze and hands, and the human forgets the giver.
Your line: remember the giver. Even the water had someone pouring it. Day four hundred fifty-one, done.

452.title: You are the Master
452.hook: too thaakur tum peh ardaas: You are the Master, to You this prayer; You are mother and father, we Your children
452.howItsDone: This stanza closes the fourth ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib; it is often said standing, just before the Ardas, and some say it quietly at night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, daataa, the giver: life, food and a body, all given, and the giver forgotten. Your line was remember the giver. Today, ashtpadi four reaches its last stanza.

A small child wakes in the night and calls out one word. Not a speech, not an explanation: just the name of the person who will come. The child doesn't wonder whether it's allowed, or whether the words are right, or whether the request is too small. It knows who to call. Ashtpadi four has spent its stanzas on the forgetful one: you were fed, clothed, carried, and you forgot. Then, in the eighth and last stanza, the voice changes. The scolding stops, and a child calls out.
screen: `A CHILD CALLS IN THE NIGHT.` → `ONE WORD, NO SPEECH.` → `THE SCOLDING STOPS.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens: too thaakur, tum peh ardaas. You are the Master; to You, this prayer. Thaakur is an old word for a lord or master, the one a household depends on. Ardaas is the word Sikhs still use for their standing prayer, said at the close of a gathering. So the first line names who God is, and says what's happening: asking. The next line, in plain words: soul and body are all Your capital, Your trust, held for a while. Then the line that gives today its carry: tum maat pitaa, ham baarik tere. You are mother and father; we are Your children. Notice the order: mother comes first. Guru Arjan reaches for an everyday bond, parent and child, and uses it for the One beyond all forms. A Master can feel far away. A mother is the one who comes when you call in the night. Next: in Your kindness are countless comforts. And the stanza holds both: the One higher than the highest, whose limit nobody knows, and the One as near as a parent's hand. The forgetful guest of the last few days isn't thrown out. The stanza ends with the guest finally speaking like a child at home. Guru Arjan closes ashtpadi four signing it Nanak, as the Gurus sign their hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib: Your servant, forever a sacrifice to You.
screen: `THAAKUR: THE MASTER OF THE HOUSE.` · `ARDAAS: TO YOU, THIS PRAYER.` · `SOUL AND BODY, ALL YOUR TRUST.` · `MOTHER AND FATHER; WE, YOUR CHILDREN.` · then, large: `MOTHER AND FATHER.`

segments.voice: Say the line once, slowly: tum maat pitaa, ham baarik tere, You are mother and father; we are Your children, as a prayer if you pray, or as a line of old poetry if you don't. Then breathe in with mother and father, breathe out with we, the children, and let your shoulders drop, the way they do when someone you trust walks into the room.
Thaakur, master or lord: too thaakur, the opening of ashtpadi four's last stanza, where the forgetful guest finally calls out like a child.
Your line: mother and father. A good last line to hear yourself say before sleep. Rest well.

453.title: Living ashtpadi 4
453.hook: many say this stanza just before Ardas
453.howItsDone: In many gurdwaras the congregation stands, palms together, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, and recites 'too thaakur tum peh ardaas' before the Ardas is led; many Sikhs also say it before their own Ardas at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thaakur: the stanza that turns the forgetful guest into a child. Your line was mother and father. Today, the same stanza, said standing.

Near the end of a gurdwara service, the whole room rises. Shoes already off, heads already covered. People stand, palms pressed together, facing the Guru Granth Sahib. Someone is about to lead the Ardas, the long standing prayer that closes the gathering. And in many gurdwaras, before the Ardas begins, the room says a stanza together. Its first words came yesterday: too thaakur, tum peh ardaas. Yesterday it was a line in a book. Today, it's a room on its feet.
screen: `THE WHOLE ROOM RISES.` → `PALMS TOGETHER, FACING THE GURU.` → `A STANZA YOU ALREADY KNOW.`

segments.voice: The Ardas is the Sikh community's prayer. It remembers God, the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib; it remembers the Sikhs who suffered and served; then it asks, for the people present and for the good of all. Most of the Ardas's wording isn't scripture. It grew up in the community and was set down in the Sikh code of conduct. But the stanza many say just before it is scripture: the eighth stanza of Sukhmani's fourth ashtpadi, Guru Arjan's words from the Guru Granth Sahib. So the room moves from the Guru's words into the community's asking. Why this stanza? Read it as a doorway. Too thaakur, tum peh ardaas: Master, to You, this prayer. That's the address on the envelope. Soul and body are all Your trust: that's who is asking, and on what terms. Nothing here is owned; all of it is held. You are mother and father, we Your children: that's the tone. Not a petition to a distant court, but a child at home. Then: nobody knows Your limit, You are highest of the high, all creation is strung on Your thread. Before anyone asks for anything, the stanza sets the size of things. The asker is small. The One asked is without end. And the asker is still loved. That's ashtpadi four, lived in a room. The stanzas before say: you forgot the giver. The last one says: turn around, stand up, and ask.
screen: `THE ARDAS: THE COMMUNITY'S PRAYER.` · `BEFORE IT, THE GURU'S OWN WORDS.` · `THE ADDRESS, THE TERMS, THE TONE.` · `THE ASKER IS SMALL, AND LOVED.` · then, large: `TO YOU, THIS PRAYER.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand, with palms together or hands at rest. If you pray, say the stanza's opening the way a gurdwara does, too thaakur, tum peh ardaas, jeeo pind sabh teree raas; if not, say the English slowly, You are the Master; soul and body are all Your trust, and notice how it feels said standing. Then feel your feet on the floor, holding you up, and breathe.
Ardaas, a prayer of asking: the stanza that ends ashtpadi four, said by many Sikhs standing, just before the Ardas, the Guru's words, then the community's asking.
Your line: to you, this prayer. First the address, then the asking. Day four hundred fifty-three.

454.title: Ashtpadi 5, salok: giving and taking
454.hook: the salok warns against clinging to gifts and forgetting the Giver
454.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani Sahib meet this salok at the start of the fifth ashtpadi; some readers take one ashtpadi a day, beginning with its salok.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ardaas: a room on its feet before the Ardas. Your line was to you, this prayer. Today, the fifth ashtpadi opens with a warning.

Hold your hand out, palm up, a coin resting on it. Now close your fist around it. Tighter. Your knuckles go white. Your whole arm is busy, and you can't pick anything else up, or wave, or shake a hand. Same coin, two ways of holding it. Ashtpadi five of Sukhmani Sahib is about those two hands, and it opens with a short couplet, a salok, about what happens when the fist forgets who put the coin there.
screen: `A COIN ON AN OPEN PALM.` → `THE SAME COIN IN A FIST.` → `TWO WAYS OF HOLDING.`

segments.voice: The salok has two lines. In the first, Guru Arjan names God denhaar, the Giver, literally the one whose nature is to give, and describes people who leave the Giver and attach themselves to other tastes, other pleasures. Not bad things, necessarily: things that were given, now held as if they made themselves. The second line, signed Nanak, says such people never truly succeed, and that without the Name their honor slips away. Notice what the salok doesn't say. It doesn't call the gifts wicked. The last ashtpadi named water, a breeze, family and hands among the gifts. The trouble starts when the gift crowds out the Giver. A few stanzas later, the ashtpadi gives a picture for it. Someone falls in love with the shade of a tree. But shade moves with the sun. It passes, and he's left with regret in his mind. The shade was real, and a gift. It just wasn't a possession. That line between giving and taking runs through this whole ashtpadi. What comes from the Giver is received. What's clung to as mine feels taken when it leaves. So the Sikh word here is not renouncing. Guru Arjan was a householder, and Sikhs are asked to live in the world. The word is holding: open palm, not fist.

455.title: Ten things and one
455.hook: given ten things, one is held back, and he loses faith
455.howItsDone: Sikhs read this stanza as part of Sukhmani Sahib, often daily; preachers in katha often use the ten-and-one picture to talk about gratitude.

segments.voice: Yesterday, denhaar: the Giver, and the open palm. Your line was hold gifts loosely. Today, at the end of a week, the first stanza of ashtpadi five does some arithmetic.

A birthday. Ten presents on the table, every one chosen with care. The child opens nine, then ten, and asks: where's the eleventh? The one I asked for? Suddenly the ten are forgotten, and the afternoon is about the one that isn't there. It's easy to laugh at that, and easy to do it, at thirty, at fifty, about a job, a body, a year. Guru Arjan put that same arithmetic into Sukhmani more than four hundred years ago, plain as a sum.
screen: `TEN PRESENTS ON THE TABLE.` → `WHERE'S THE ELEVENTH?` → `A SCENE AS PLAIN AS A SUM.`

segments.voice: The stanza begins: das basatoo lai paachhai paavai. He takes ten things and puts them behind him. Das is ten; basatoo, things, gifts. Paachhai paavai: puts them at his back, out of sight. Then: ek basat kaaran bikhot gavaavai. For the sake of one thing, he throws away his trust. Commentators read that last word slightly differently, losing faith, losing credit, being shown as faithless, but the picture holds. Ten received, one withheld, and the ten disappear behind the one. Ten against one isn't close. It's not a story about someone treated unfairly; it's about attention. The missing thing sits in front of the eyes, and the ten slip behind the back, still there, still given, just unseen. That's why this stanza follows a salok about the Giver. The ingratitude it describes isn't loud or rude. It's quiet, ordinary, and it happens by turning around. And the week ends here. Six days ago, the third ashtpadi asked for the Name and deeds to match. Then the fourth: remember who made you; the ungrateful guest; the child calling out, You are mother and father, to You this prayer. Then the fifth: the Giver, the open palm, and now ten things and one. One lesson from three sides. The gifts were always there. The question is which way you're facing.
screen: `DAS BASATOO: TEN THINGS.` · `PUT BEHIND HIS BACK.` · `ONE HELD BACK, AND TRUST GOES.` · `THE TEN, STILL THERE, UNSEEN.` · then, large: `TEN GIVEN, ONE HELD BACK.`

segments.voice: Count ten things you've been given on your fingers, small and real: the breath you're taking, water from a tap, someone who answered a message, your eyes, a bed. If the missing thing pushes in, notice it and let it stand at the back for once; then rest your two full hands in your lap and breathe with them.
Das basatoo, ten things: das basatoo lai paachhai paavai, given ten, one held back, and the ten are put behind the back.
Your line: ten given, one held back. The table was full all along. A week, done.
